title: EXAMINATION: L.S.V (W01895659)

I. Summary of the facts
On 27/02/2026 the Office issued a Notification of ex officio provisional refusal of protection
pursuant to Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2) EUTMR because it found that the trade
mark applied for is descriptive and devoid of any distinctive character.
The goods for which the provisional refusal was issued were:
Class 7 Agricultural machines and implements; robots used in agriculture; agricultural
cultivators; mowing and reaping machines; agricultural seed planting
machines; harvesting machines; weeding machines; self-propelled road
sweeping machines; snow ploughs.
Class 12 Automobiles; electric cars; hybrid cars; self-driving cars; electric vehicles;
electrically powered motor vehicles; self-propelled electric vehicles; electric
personal mobility motor vehicles; quadricycles; electric quadricycles; four-
wheeled electrically powered scooters; motor vehicles with four-wheel drive;
compact motor vehicles with four-wheel drive; self-balancing electric cars;
self-balancing electrically powered four-wheeled vehicles; self-balancing
motor vehicles; self-balancing cars; autonomous cars; robotic cars;
autonomous land vehicles; driverless cars; remotely controlled land vehicles
for transport; self-driving robots for delivery; outdoor self-driving robots for
package delivery; automatic guided vehicles; traction engine; exploration
vehicle for extreme environment; tires; tires for land vehicles; parts and
fittings of automobiles; parts and fittings of electric cars; parts and fittings of
hybrid cars; parts and fittings of self-driving cars; parts and fittings of electric

vehicles; parts and fittings of electrically powered motor vehicles; parts and

compact motor vehicles with four-wheel drive; parts and fittings of self-

powered four-wheeled vehicles; parts and fittings of self-balancing motor
vehicles; parts and fittings of self-balancing cars; parts and fittings of
autonomous cars; parts and fittings of robotic cars; parts and fittings of
autonomous land vehicles; parts and fittings of driverless cars; parts and
fittings of remotely controlled land vehicles for transport; parts and fittings of
self-driving robots for delivery; parts and fittings of outdoor self-driving robots
for package delivery; parts and fittings of automatic guided vehicles; parts
and fittings of traction engine; parts and fittings of exploration vehicle for
extreme environment; non-electric prime movers for land vehicles, not
including their parts; engines for land vehicles; engine mounts for land
vehicles; driving motors for land vehicles; motors for land vehicles; jet
engines for land vehicles; propulsion mechanisms for land vehicles;
propulsion mechanisms for motor vehicles; propulsion mechanisms for
quadricycles; mechanical elements for land vehicles; shafts, axles or
spindles, machine elements for land vehicles; bearings, machine elements for
land vehicles; shaft couplings, machine elements for land vehicles; power
transmissions and gearing, machine elements for land vehicles; shock
absorbers, machine elements for land vehicles; springs, machine elements
for land vehicles; brakes, machine elements for land vehicles; vehicles for the
physically handicapped and those of reduced mobility; vehicles for people
with mobility difficulties; parts and fittings of vehicles for the physically
handicapped and those of reduced mobility; parts and fittings of vehicles for
people with mobility difficulties; AC motors or DC motors for land vehicles, not
including their parts.
The grounds for refusal were based on the following main findings:
• How descriptiveness is assessed depends on how the relevant consumer would
perceive the sign in relation to the goods and services for which protection is sought.
In this case, the relevant English-speaking consumer would understand the sign as
having the following meaning: Low-Speed Vehicle, a type of four-wheeled motorized
vehicle typically designed for operation at speeds lower than 40 kilometers per hour,
and for running short distances.
• The above-mentioned meaning of the acronym ‘L.S.V’, of which the trade mark
consists, is supported by the following dictionary and internet references:
L.S.V. ‘Low-Speed Vehicle’ (information extracted from the online dictionary
Acronym Finder on 27/02/2026 at https://www.acronymfinder.com/LSV.html ).
‘A Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) is a type of motorized vehicle intentionally
designed for operation at speeds lower than those of conventional passenger
vehicles. LSVs often run on electric power and are primarily intended for short
distance travel within controlled environments. Typically designed for

Page 3 of 11
roadways with a maximum speed of 35 mph or less , LSVs offer an
economical and ecofriendly transportation solution for various purposes.
These environments encompass gated communities, campuses, resorts,
industrial complexes, and specific urban areas. Because they are street legal
in these designated zones, LSVs are equipped with safety features such as
parking brakes and adhere to a maximum speed that is 25 mph, considerably
lower than typical traffic speeds on public roads. One distinguishing
characteristic between LSVs and golf carts is that non-golf-only vehicles are
assigned a unique vehicle identification number, similar to the vehicle
identification number in practice for standard vehicles. While they might
resemble golf carts, LSVs serve broader purposes beyond the golf course. As
four-wheeled vehicles, they align with safety requirements and regulations
that permit their operation within confined regions of public roads. LSVs must
also operate within the confines of the posted speed limit, ensuring the safety
of both operators and pedestrians’ (information extracted from the LSP
provider Westward Industries on 27/02/2026 at
https://westwardindustries.com/low-speed-vehiclelsv/the-definition-of-lsv/).
The relevant consumers would perceive the sign as providing information that
the machines, apparatus and vehicles applied for in Classes 7 and 12 to
which an objection has been raised, and the parts and fittings therefor applied
for in Class 12 consist of four-wheeled vehicles, that can be electrical, self-
propelled or driven by humans, and which normally have lower weight than
normal cars and have stricter speed limits, normally of up to 30-40 kilometres
per hour. Therefore, the sign describes the kind of the goods.
• Given that the sign has a clear descriptive meaning, it is also devoid of any distinctive
character and therefore ineligible for registration under Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR. This
means that it is incapable of performing the essential function of a trade mark, which
is to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other
undertakings.
• Furthermore, signs that are commonly used in connection with the marketing of the
goods concerned are devoid of distinctive character for those goods. In this context,
an internet search dated 27/02/2026 revealed that the acronym ‘L.S.V’ is
commonly used in the relevant market:
1. https://www.machinerytrader.ie/listing/for-sale/253413603/2016-polaris-
gemem1400- lsv-utility-utility-vehicles
2. https://www.farmandplant.ie/listings/for-sale/club-car/urban-lsv/utility-vehicles-
utvslash-atv-slash-bikes/1171
3. https://www.alke.com/road-legal-low-speed-vehicles-lsv
• The fact that the acronym contains the dots between the letters does not add any
distinctive character. Acronyms are commonly written both with dots per each
abbreviated letter, or without them and consumers will not assign any specific
commercial origin significance but rather the use of dots will be seen as a
grammatical feature of the acronym itself (information extracted from the online
grammar resource Grammar Monster on 27/02/2026at https://www.grammar-
monster.com/lessons/abbreviations_full_stops_periods.htm).

Page 4 of 11
• Consequently, taken as a whole, the sign is descriptive and devoid of distinctive
character. It is therefore incapable of distinguishing the goods for which an objection
has been raised under Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2) EUTMR.
In addition, the holder was requested to appoint a representative entitled to represent third
parties before the Office, pursuant to Articles 119(2) and 120(1) EUTMR.
II. Summary of the holder’s arguments
The holder submitted its observations on 27/04/2026, which may be summarised as follows:
1. The sign is not descriptive of the goods. It is arguable whether the relevant public
will immediately perceive L.S.V. as meaning a low-speed vehicle. The holder
questions how it describes the kind of goods and how it will automatically mean
‘Low Speed Vehicle’.
2. The holder gives an analysis of the English-speaking population within the
European Union and provides that only 2% of the EU population has English as a
first language. It also points to L.S.V. having more meanings. It points to the holder
intending to use the L.S.V to mean ‘Lean steer Vehicle’. The Office has not proved
the sign is descriptive across all the European Union.
3. The Office has not defined the consumer of the goods, except for noting that they
are English-speaking. It considers that it is unlikely that the niche public would buy
the holder’s L.S.V. branded products and expect that they are ‘low speed vehicle’
products. The objection is excessively broad and did not consider every objected
good.
4. The sign is distinctive. It is not descriptive so cannot rely on that argument for not
being distinctive. The sign has been accepted at the UKIPO.
III. Reasons
Pursuant to Article 94 EUTMR, it is up to the Office to take a decision based on reasons or
evidence on which the holder has had an opportunity to present its comments.
After giving due consideration to the holder's arguments, the Office has decided to waive the
grounds for refusal for the following goods:
Class 7 Agricultural machines and implements; Robots used in agriculture;
Agricultural cultivators; Mowing and reaping machines; Agricultural seed
planting machines; Harvesting machines; Weeding machines; Self-propelled
road sweeping machines; Snow ploughs.
The grounds for refusal are maintained for the remaining goods.
General comments:

Page 5 of 11
Under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR, ‘trade marks which consist exclusively of signs or indications
which may serve, in trade, to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value,
geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or of rendering of the service, or
other characteristics of the goods or service’ are not to be registered.
By prohibiting the registration as European Union trade marks of the signs and indications to
which it refers, Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR
pursues an aim which is in the public interest, namely that descriptive signs or
indications relating to the characteristics of goods or services in respect of which
registration is sought may be freely used by all. That provision accordingly
prevents such signs and indications from being reserved to one undertaking
alone because they have been registered as trade marks.
(23/10/2003, C-191/01 P, Doublemint, EU:C:2003:579, § 31).
‘The signs and indications referred to in Article 7(1)(c) [EUTMR] are those which may serve
in normal usage from the point of view of the target public to designate, either directly or by
reference to one of their essential characteristics, the goods or service in respect of which
registration is sought’ (26/11/2003, T-222/02, Robotunits, EU:T:2003:315, § 34).
For a sign to be caught by the prohibition set out in that provision, there must be a
sufficiently direct and specific relationship between the sign and the goods and services in
question to enable the public concerned immediately to perceive, without further thought, a
description of the goods and services in question or of one of their characteristics
(22/06/2005, T-19/04, Paperlab, EU:T:2005:247, § 25; 27/02/2002, T-106/00, Streamserve,
EU:T:2002:43, § 40).
The descriptiveness of a sign can only be assessed, first, in relation to how the relevant
public understands the sign and, second, in relation to the goods or services concerned
(13/11/2008, T-346/07, Easycover, EU:T:2008:496, § 42; 22/11/2018, T-9/18,
STRAIGHTFORWARD BANKING, EU:T:2018:827, § 18).
As to the holder’s arguments:
1. For a trade mark to be refused registration under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR, it is not
necessary that the signs and indications composing the mark that are referred to in
that article actually be in use at the time of the application for registration in a way
that is descriptive of goods or services such as those in relation to which the
application is filed, or of characteristics of those goods or services. It is sufficient,
as the wording of that provision itself indicates, that such signs and indications
could be used for such purposes. A sign must therefore be refused registration
under that provision if at least one of its possible meanings designates a
characteristic of the goods or services concerned. (23/10/2003, C 191/01 P,
Doublemint, EU:C:2003:579, § 32, emphasis added). There is no doubt that the
English-speaking public, in the market for an L.S.V. (low speed vehicle’ and when
confronted with the objected goods will naturally see them as being or being
suitable for a low-speed vehicle.
Indeed, for a trade mark to be refused registration under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR, it
is not necessary that the signs and indications composing the mark that are
referred to in that article actually be in use at the time of the application for
registration in a way that is descriptive of goods or services such as those in
relation to which the application is filed, or of characteristics of those goods or

Page 6 of 11
services. It is sufficient, as the wording of that provision itself indicates, that such
signs and indications could be used for such purposes. A sign must therefore be
refused registration under that provision if at least one of its possible meanings
designates a characteristic of the goods or services concerned. (23/10/2003,
C-191/01 P, Doublemint, EU:C:2003:579, § 32, emphasis added.)
Therefore as the consumer, in the market for a “low speed vehicle” will understand
the acronym as such, and the evidence supplied in the objection letter points to
this, including on an Irish website, then this is sufficient reason to refuse it on the
grounds of descriptiveness.
2. Article 7(1) EUTMR is a provision under European Union (EU) law and has to be
interpreted on the basis of a common EU standard. However, Article 7(2) EUTMR
excludes an application from registration if a ground for refusal exists even in only
part of the EU. Therefore, it is sufficient for a refusal if the trade mark is descriptive
or lacks distinctive character in any one of the official EU languages (03/07/2013,
T 236/12, Neo, EU:T:2013:343, § 57).
Regarding the argument that the sign is not descriptive for the majority of EU
consumers, it has to be held that, whilst Article 7(1) EUTMR is a legal provision
under European Union (EU) law and has to be interpreted on the basis of a
common EU standard. However, Article 7(2) EUTMR excludes an application from
registration if a ground for refusal exists even only in part of the EU. Therefore,
even if the sign is not descriptive for most EU consumers, it is sufficient for a
refusal if it is descriptive, or lacks distinctive character, in any one of the official EU
languages (03/07/2013, T 236/12, Neo, EU:T:2013:343, § 57).
Accordingly, the fact that the sign is descriptive and non-distinctive for English-
speaking consumers within the EU is sufficient for it to be refused under Article
7(1) EUTMR.
3. The Office has already shown that the English-speaking consumer, in the market
for a Low Velocity Vehicle will see L.S.V. as such. Even if the consumer is from a
smaller subset of the English-speaking consumer group, including farmers or
estate owners or golf course or hotel resort owners, terms that have a specific
technical meaning can also be descriptive of characteristics of the goods. In such
cases, it does not have to be demonstrated that the meaning of the term is
immediately apparent to all relevant consumers to which the goods/services may
be addressed. It is sufficient that the term is meant to be used, or could be
understood by part of the relevant public, as a description or characteristic of the
goods/services for which protection is sought (18/11/2015, T 558/14,
TRILOBULAR, EU:T:2015:858, § 23, 50).
As the Office has already shown in the explanations and evidence in the objection
letter, the sign can be understood at least by those in the market for a low velocity
vehicle in a descriptive way, this is sufficient to justify a refusal under Article 7(1)(c)
EUTMR.
The holder considers that the Office has been very broad in its objection and has
not considered all goods. In principle, any characteristic of the goods and services
must lead to a refusal under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR. It does not matter whether the
characteristics of the goods or services are commercially essential or merely
ancillary or whether there are synonyms of them. In the light of the public interest
underlying the provision, any undertaking must be able freely to use such signs
and indications to describe any characteristic whatsoever of its own goods,

Page 7 of 11
irrespective of how significant the characteristic may be commercially (12/02/2004,
C-363/99, Postkantoor, EU:C:2004:86, § 102; 24/04/2012, T-328/11, EcoPerfect,
EU:T:2012:197, § 41).
The auxiliary goods, for example such as tires, parts and fitting and power
transmissions and gearing in Class 12 are directly linked to the actual vehicles to
which the descriptive meaning applies, because the former are typically offered in
conjunction with, or involved in the use of, the latter; in particular, they will be of a
certain size or capability that will site the needs of a low speed vehicle. If the
descriptive meaning applies to an activity involving the use of several goods or
services mentioned separately in the specification, then the objection applies for all
of them (20/03/2002, T 355/00, Tele Aid, EU:T:2002:79).
4. Under Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR, ‘trade marks which are devoid of any distinctive
character’ are not to be registered.
The trade marks referred to in Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR are, in particular, those that
do not enable the relevant public ‘to repeat the experience (of a purchase), if it
proves to be positive, or to avoid it, if it proves to be negative, on the occasion of a
subsequent acquisition’ of the goods or services concerned (27/02/2002, T 79/00,
Lite, EU:T:2002:42, § 26). This is the case for, inter alia, signs commonly used in
the marketing of the goods or services concerned (15/09/2005, T 320/03, Live
richly, EU:T:2005:325, § 65).
It is established case-law that ‘[a] sign’s distinctiveness can be assessed only by
reference, first, to the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought
and, second, to the relevant public’s perception of that sign’ (09/10/2002, T
360/00, UltraPlus, EU:T:2002:244, § 43).
The Office showed evidence of the use of LSV in the relevant market and this
supports the argument that the sign is also non distinctive in its own right.
Although, in fact, the Court has confirmed that it is not up to the Office to show that
other similar signs are used on the market: [W]here the Board of Appeal finds that
the trade mark sought is devoid of intrinsic distinctive character, it may base its
analysis on facts arising from practical experience generally acquired from the
marketing of general consumer goods which are likely to be known by anyone and
are in particular known by the consumers of those goods … In such a case, the
Board of Appeal is not obliged to give examples of such practical
experience.(15/03/2006, T-129/04, Plastikflaschenform, EU:T:2006:84, § 19).
It is on the basis of such acquired experience that the Office submits that the
relevant consumers would perceive the sign applied for as non-distinctive and not
as the trade mark of a particular proprietor. Since, despite the Office’s analysis
based on such experience, the holder claims that the trade mark applied for is
distinctive, it is up to the holder to provide specific and substantiated information to
show that the trade mark applied for has distinctive character, either intrinsically or
acquired through use; it is much better placed to do so, given its thorough
knowledge of the market (05/03/2003, T-194/01, Soap device, EU:T:2003:53,
§ 48).
The applicant argues that it uses the trade mark in the market (where it stands for
Lean Steer Vehicle). However, the mere fact that a sign has been used on the
market says nothing at all about its inherent distinctiveness or how it will be
perceived and understood by actual consumers.

Page 8 of 11
The documents submitted by the holder have failed to convince the Office that the
sign applied for is capable of duly functioning as an indication of origin despite its
inherent lack of distinctive character ab initio. The documents show only that there
is logic to a vehicle having a system which prevents it from toppling over, but it is
not sufficient to convince the Office that the consumer, in the market for a low-
speed vehicle will not see L.S.V. as referring to such a vehicle.
As regards the UKIPO decision referred to by the holder, according to case-law:
the European Union trade mark regime is an autonomous system with its own set
of objectives and rules peculiar to it; it is self-sufficient and applies independently
of any national system … Consequently, the registrability of a sign as a European
Union trade mark must be assessed by reference only to the relevant Union rules.
Accordingly, the Office and, if appropriate, the Union judicature are not bound by a
decision given in a Member State, or indeed a third country, that the sign in
question is registrable as a national mark. That is so even if such a decision was
adopted under national legislation harmonised with Directive 89/104 or in a country
belonging to the linguistic area in which the word sign in question originated.
(27/02/2002, T 106/00, Streamserve, EU:T:2002:43, § 47).
Therefore, when assessing the case, the Office is not bound by the decision
referred to by the holder.
IV. Conclusion
For the abovementioned reasons, and pursuant to Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2)
EUTMR, protection of the international registration No 1895659 is partially refused for the
European Union, namely for:
Class 12 Automobiles; electric cars; hybrid cars; self-driving cars; electric vehicles;
electrically powered motor vehicles; self-propelled electric vehicles; electric
personal mobility motor vehicles; quadricycles; electric quadricycles; four-
wheeled electrically powered scooters; motor vehicles with four-wheel drive;

According to Article 67 EUTMR, you have a right to appeal against this decision. According
to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of appeal must be filed in writing at the Office within two months
of the date of notification of this decision. It must be filed in the language of the proceedings
